lead: An Android project is a small, fixed set of files. You edit XML for text and layout, Java for behaviour, and a manifest for app identity. The build turns each XML file and string into an integer constant in a generated class called R. Java then uses R.layout.activity_main or R.string.greeting, not file names. This separates design from code and catches missing resources at build time. Every Android app uses it. Only a few universities teach this depth.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.2 for the SDK and API level.

blocks.text: A new project called HelloApp has one app module. The module folder holds four things you touch first. manifests/AndroidManifest.xml names the app and its first activity. java/.../MainActivity.java is the screen's Java class. res/layout/activity_main.xml is the view tree. res/values/strings.xml holds text. build.gradle holds module settings: SDK levels, dependencies and app ID. The top-level build.gradle is separate; the module one decides how this app is built. In the New Project wizard choose Java as the language (and Groovy DSL if offered), so the module file is build.gradle and the activity is MainActivity.java. Kotlin projects follow the same anatomy, with .kt files and build.gradle.kts.

AndroidManifest.xml is not optional. For the first screen it needs an activity with the MAIN action and LAUNCHER category. Without that pair, the app installs but no icon opens it. MainActivity.java extends AppCompatActivity, which itself extends Activity, and overrides onCreate in both cases. setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) makes Android inflate the XML view tree. Add findViewById(R.id.text1) only when Java must change a view at run time. The package name, here com.example.hello, gives R its full name.

During a build, Gradle runs AAPT2, the Android asset packaging tool. AAPT2 compiles each resource file. It gives every layout, string, drawable and view ID an integer constant. It writes these constants into R.java, generated in the app's package, for example com.example.hello.R. You never type or edit R.java. It contains nested classes: R.layout, R.id, R.string.

R.layout.activity_main is an int, not a file path. R.id.button1 is an int, not a button. R.string.greeting is an int, not text. At run time the framework uses the int to look up the compiled resource in the APK. In XML, @+id/button1 creates an ID; @id/button1 refers to an existing one; @string/greeting refers to a string resource. A bad @string name leaves no constant, so Java shows a red R. That is a resource error, not a missing import.

Start an emulator from Device Manager. Press Run. Gradle builds a debug APK, installs it, and sends a launch intent naming the launcher activity. Android creates MainActivity, calls onCreate, and setContentView inflates res/layout/activity_main.xml. The TextView reads @string/greeting and shows Hello, Chennai. Log.d("HelloApp", "onCreate") writes to Logcat. Open Logcat and filter by tag HelloApp or package com.example.hello. If the app stops, the top line is usually the exception.

Use a real phone the same way after enabling USB debugging. The build must finish before install starts; a failed build leaves the old APK running, which looks like an ignored edit. Check the Run window for BUILD SUCCESSFUL. Clear Logcat before a fresh run; old lines mislead. A crash on launch usually points to the manifest (activity not declared, wrong theme) or to findViewById returning null because the id is missing from the inflated layout. A missing layout file stops the build instead.

figure.caption: The app module is the unit you build. The manifest names the launcher activity, java holds behaviour, res holds XML resources, and build.gradle sets module options.

spec.aria: A project folder tree with HelloApp holding the app module, which holds manifests, java sources, resources and the module build file.

examples.question: A new project is HelloApp, package com.example.hello, one empty activity. You must show Hello, Chennai. (a) Name the two files you edit and the exact change in each. (b) State how many files are edited. (c) State the manifest condition for the app to open.
steps: res/values/strings.xml: add a string resource named greeting with value Hello, Chennai. AAPT2 will make R.string.greeting.
res/layout/activity_main.xml: add a TextView with id text1 and text set to @string/greeting. This creates R.id.text1 and uses R.string.greeting.

MainActivity.java: leave it unchanged. The template already calls setContentView(R.layout.activity_main), which inflates activity_main, so the TextView appears with the greeting. findViewById(R.id.text1) is needed only to change the text at run time.
Manifest: not edited here, but its activity needs MAIN and LAUNCHER, or no icon opens the app.
examples.answer: Two files are edited: strings.xml and activity_main.xml. MainActivity.java is untouched; its existing setContentView(R.layout.activity_main) inflates the layout, and the TextView takes its text from @string/greeting. The manifest must declare the launcher activity with MAIN and LAUNCHER.

traps: Editing XML and expecting the running app to change without a rebuild. Resources are compiled into R and the APK.
No import of R is needed, because R sits in the app's own package com.example.hello. The harmful one is import android.R. A red R almost always means a resource error somewhere, not a missing import.
Confusing @+id/button1 (creates an ID) with @id/button1 (refers to one).
Missing MAIN and LAUNCHER: the app installs but no launcher icon opens it.
Calling findViewById before setContentView returns null.

quiz.a: A generated class of int resource constants.

quiz.q: Why are R.layout.activity_main and R.id.text1 ints, not file names?
quiz.a: Resources are compiled into an indexed APK table; ints give fast lookup and build-time checks.

quiz.q: A TextView has id text1 and text set to @string/greeting. Which R constants appear?
Give the Java call order in onCreate to show a layout, then change a TextView.
The app installs but no icon opens it. What manifest entry is missing?
quiz.a: An activity with MAIN action and LAUNCHER category.

quiz.q: R.string.greeting turns red after an XML rename. Why?
quiz.a: AAPT2 no longer generates that constant; fix the XML key or Java reference and rebuild.

beyond: Not for the exam. Android Studio hides most AAPT2 calls behind Gradle, but the same int constants appear in the APK resource table. Modern apps often use Jetpack Compose, which builds UI in Kotlin instead of XML; the manifest and R class still exist for resources. Search 'AAPT2 compile link', 'R.java generated', and 'Android resource shrinking' to go deeper.
